projects.title: LoadForge
projects.tags: AWS · Terraform · NestJS · Next.js · k6 · GitHub Actions
projects.summary: A self-built lab for learning AWS: load-test an auto-scaling Node.js fleet, then harden it step by step.
details: Provisioned the whole stack with Terraform: VPC, HTTPS load balancer, EC2 Auto Scaling with CloudWatch alarms, keyless GitHub OIDC deploys
Three apps: the servers under test (NestJS), a watcher that streams the Auto Scaling group and CloudWatch over SSE, and a Next.js dashboard
Raised throughput by 47% (26.7 → 39.2 req/s), cut health-check latency under load from ~20 s to 8 ms and scale-out from ~3 min to 30–50 s
Every change measured with a k6 load generator, shipped through zero-downtime CI/CD

caseStudy.context: A lab I built on my own time to learn AWS by putting it under load: a fleet of Node.js servers (the Defenders) in an EC2 Auto Scaling group behind an HTTPS load balancer, a Watcher that streams the group's state, and a dashboard that shows it and runs load tests. All provisioned with Terraform and shipped through GitHub Actions.
caseStudy.problem: Auto scaling looks simple on paper: add a server when average CPU passes 60%. The point was to load-test the real thing, find each place it failed to hold up, fix it, and measure every change.
approach: Provisioned the stack with Terraform: a VPC across 2 public subnets, an HTTPS load balancer with a wildcard certificate, a launch template, the Auto Scaling group, CloudWatch, and config in SSM Parameter Store
Scaling rule: target tracking on average CPU at 60%
A CPU-heavy route on the Defenders (counting primes) to take traffic from k6 or the dashboard's own load test
Zero-downtime deploys: GitHub Actions builds the images to GHCR, and instance refresh starts new servers before stopping old ones

chapters.title: Half the CPU went unused
chapters.problem: Under load, the group never scaled out.
chapters.why: A t3.micro has 2 vCPUs, but Node.js runs JavaScript on one core. One core sat at 100% and the other near 0%, so average CPU topped out around 50% and never reached the 60% target.
fix: Node cluster: one worker per vCPU sharing the port, with the primary process restarting any that die
chapters.result: CPU use 101% → 200% and throughput 26.7 → 39.2 req/s (+47%). The scaling rule can fire.

chapters.title: Busy servers were replaced as dead
chapters.problem: Under heavy load, servers were terminated and replaced instead of the group growing.
chapters.why: The load balancer's health check waited in line behind the CPU-heavy requests on the same workers. It took ~20 s, timed out, and a server that was only busy was marked unhealthy.
fix: The primary process answers health checks on its own port, while the load stays on the workers
Keep-alive raised to 125 s, past the load balancer's 120 s, which ended random 502s from reused closed connections
chapters.result: At 200% CPU the health check answers in 8 ms, and busy servers stay in the group.

chapters.title: The dashboard went blind during tests
chapters.problem: During a load test the dashboard froze, and when it did show data, the data was minutes old.
chapters.why: Its live stream was served by the same workers that ran the load, and CloudWatch data arrives 1–2 minutes late.
fix: A separate Watcher service streams to the dashboard, polling only while one is open, since CloudWatch reads are billed
Each Defender keeps its own last 5 minutes at one point per second and its last hour in 15 s steps; the Watcher reads them directly
CloudWatch only fills the gaps, such as servers that are already gone
chapters.result: Dashboard delay 2–3 minutes → a few seconds, every point measured and none filled in.

chapters.title: Three minutes to react to a spike
chapters.problem: A burst pushes the first server past 90% CPU at once, but the 60% rule waits for 3 one-minute data points before adding a server, and that server still has to boot.
fix: A second, danger level: each server publishes its CPU every 10 s, and an average over 90% for 30 s adds 2 servers at once
New servers boot from an image with Docker already installed, so boot skips installing it
chapters.result: Scaling out starts in 30–50 s instead of about 3 minutes, for around $0.60 a month.

chapters.title: Traffic wasn't shared evenly
chapters.problem: Once new servers were ready, the load balancer still sent the overloaded one the same share of new requests.
chapters.why: Round robin takes turns; it doesn't look at how busy each server is.
fix: Switched the target group to least outstanding requests: each new request goes to the server with the fewest still in flight
chapters.result: New servers take most new requests until they are as busy as the rest, while the overloaded one drains.

results: Health check under load ~20 s → 8 ms
Dashboard delay 2–3 minutes → a few seconds
Deploys with no downtime, even on a single server
open: Per-IP rate limiting with AWS WAF: against a real attacker, scaling means paying to serve the attack
A warm pool of pre-booted servers that start in 20–30 s
The app image baked into the server image, so boot skips the pull too
At least 2 servers at all times, so one isn't a single point of failure
Load shedding: answer 503 fast once a server's queue is too long
Measure boot time before and after the image change

projects.title: Coding Guide
projects.tags: Claude Code · MCP · Next.js · Strapi · AWS
projects.summary: Claude Code skills distilled from lessons on client projects, used in daily work.
details: A review checklist built from the bugs that came up most often across projects, checked against every change
Bug-fix workflow automated via ClickUp MCP: fix, self-review, open pull requests and report back, with human approval at each step
One-command setup for new Next.js + Strapi projects, wired to the client's technical criteria
EC2 deploy playbooks (Docker + GHCR, and PM2) that record every mistake made on the first production run
General UI/UX rules with a review checklist for building and reviewing screens

caseStudy.context: My own set of Claude Code skills: the rules, checklists and workflows I kept re-explaining on client projects, written down once so an AI agent and I apply them the same way every time. Public on GitHub, and used in my daily work.
caseStudy.problem: The same bugs kept coming back on new projects, and each project learnt them again. A lesson that lives in a commit message or in one repo's notes doesn't survive the next project, and an AI agent without that context repeats the mistake with full confidence.
approach: Went through the history of two client projects, 578 commits and 84 tickets, and turned what had to be fixed into a review checklist: 199 checks in 12 sections, each linked to the commit that fixed it
Wrote each check to say how to see the problem, because most of them fail silently: a CMS field the API ignores, a CSS class that emits nothing, a fallback that looks exactly like real content
Made reviews load only the sections a change can affect, so a typical branch is checked against 3 or 4 of the 12 sections instead of the whole list
Automated the bug-fix workflow through ClickUp MCP: read the queue, sort it, fix, review against the checklist, ship to staging and report on each ticket, pausing for approval where asked
Turned new-project setup into one skill wired to the client's 33 technical criteria, and wrote deploy and SEO playbooks from building this site
results: 7 skills, public on GitHub and in daily use
Every check can be traced back to the bug and the commit behind it
This site was deployed and given its SEO with these skills, and its first production run added its own mistakes to the deploy playbook
open: The PM2 deploy playbook has not been run end to end yet
